What does poverty look like beyond income?

Someone can live above an income poverty line and still go without electricity, clean drinking water, or schooling.

The global Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI), from the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative and the UN Development Programme, counts the deprivations people face at the same time. We recently updated our 16 charts with the 2026 release, published in October, which adds new surveys for 13 countries.

The MPI looks at ten indicators in three areas, using data from household surveys: health (nutrition and child mortality), education (years of schooling and school attendance), and living standards (cooking fuel, sanitation, drinking water, electricity, housing, and assets). People deprived in a third or more of the weighted indicators count as “multidimensionally poor”. You can read more about how the MPI works in our article.

The chart shows this for Nigeria, which has a new survey from 2024. About half of Nigerians live in a household without electricity, about half in one without adequate sanitation, and more than three-quarters in one that cooks with solid fuels like wood or charcoal. 12% live in a household where a child has died in the previous five years.

(This data update was led by @parriagadap.)

note_tweet.text:
MaxIM: Maximally Informative Incremental Summarization via Reinforcement Learning : https://t.co/8uYmlbqq3D

"arXiv:2611.12825v1 [https://t.co/gQRNwvACTl] 09 Nov 2026
MaxIM: Maximally Informative Incremental Summarization via Reinforcement Learning
Jihwan JeongGoogle ResearchGuy TennenholtzWork done while at Google.NoetiveYinlam ChowGoogle DeepMind{jihwanjeong, yinlamchow, cwhsu, cboutilier}@google.com, guytenn@gmail.comChih-Wei HsuGoogle ResearchCraig BoutilierGoogle ResearchAbstract
AI systems must often maintain bounded memory of unbounded interaction histories. However, optimizing the memory representation, and its updates, for downstream task utility is difficult for standard reinforcement learning (RL) due to severe credit assignment bottlenecks induced by sparse, delayed rewards. We introduce MaxIM (Maximally Informative Incremental Memory), a framework that formulates incremental summarization as a capacity-constrained, information-theoretic reward-shaping problem. Grounded in value suboptimality bounds, we show that bounding sequential information loss motivates maximizing the predictive log-likelihood of future, task-relevant targets, a variational lower bound on predictive sufficiency. We introduce a recursive consistency condition to ensure summaries are grounded by maximizing mutual information (MI) with the observed history. We mitigate credit assignment issues with a parameterized asymmetric critic that computes step-wise variational MI bounds for dense reward shaping. Empirical evaluation on long-horizon scientific reading and multi-turn dialogue benchmarks shows that MaxIM outperforms RL, supervised fine-tuning, and prompt-focused baselines on factual grounding, comprehensive autorater metrics, and downstream task utility across strict token budgets and extended horizons, without the need for expensive human preference labels.
1Introduction
A critical challenge facing AI agents in continuous, streaming environments—from real-time personalization [1, 2] to long-horizon dialogue [3, 4]—is the inability to retain unbounded context. Despite the expanded context windows of modern large language models (LLMs), processing ever-growing interaction logs frequently degrades reasoning performance due to “lost in the middle” phenomena [5]. While heuristic memory buffers (e.g., MemGPT [6]) and RL-based memory models (e.g., MemAgent [7], Mem-α [8]) offer practical mechanisms for context management, agents ultimately need rigorous methods to actively compress these streams into a fixed-capacity working memory.We assume a trainable history/context summarization policy manages this bounded memory state, while a separate, frozen action agent uses it to choose how to act in the environment. In this setting, the objective of a memory system is to maximize downstream task utility, Rtask. In principle, optimizing a summarizer using reinforcement learning (RL) on Rtask yields an optimal compression strategy. However, in long-horizon settings, task rewards are notoriously sparse and delayed, inducing extreme credit assignment failures in RL—the policy receives insufficiently granular feedback to learn which observation-stream features are predictive of task success. Conversely, optimizing for surface-level text reconstruction [9, 10] discards deeper latent intents needed for effective future inference.Figure 1:The MaxIM framework. Streaming Inference (Solid Lines): A trained actor policy incrementally compresses prior summaries zt−1 and incoming observations ot into a bounded memory zt. This memory, alongside recent observations, provides the context for a frozen downstream agent interacting with the environment with zero critic calls at test time. Asymmetric Training (Dotted Lines): During training, a pretrained critic qϕ evaluates the actor’s summary using oracle context Yt and the immediate history (zt−1,ot). It computes dense, information-theoretic shaping rewards (predictive sufficiency and recursive consistency) that step-wise guide the policy, bypassing the credit assignment bottleneck of the sparse terminal task reward Rtask.
To bridge this gap, we develop MaxIM (Maximally Informative Incremental Memory), a novel RL framework that addresses credit assignment with dense information-theoretic reward shaping. Leveraging bounds from state abstraction theory, we show that the performance gap induced by constrained memory is bounded by sequential information loss. We show that bounding this loss motivates maximizing the predictive log-likelihood of future, task-relevant target variables Yt, a variational lower bound on predictive sufficiency. However, optimizing an LLM purely for future prediction can induce severe hallucinations (i.e., fabricating plausible-sounding text that aligns with the task/target, but is disconnected from actual observations). To prevent this, we derive a recursive consistency regularizer that maximizes the mutual information (MI) with the immediate history, substantially suppressing ungrounded https://t.co/OPwkoU1mmh optimize this dual-objective, MaxIM employs RL with asymmetric context (see Figure 1). We leverage synthetic datasets to train a parameterized critic using supervised cross-entropy minimization, which computes step-wise baseline-normalized variational predictive likelihood (VPL) bounds [11], thus providing dense shaping rewards to the policy. We update the policy using standard policy gradient methods equipped with a backward-discounted reward-to-go to account for temporal error accumulation, while gradually annealing the shaping weight to ensure that late-stage training directly optimizes downstream task utility.Our contributions are: (1) We develop MaxIM, a principled RL framework for capacity-constrained generative memory that solves the sparse credit assignment bottleneck via dense information-theoretic reward shaping. (2) We link value suboptimality bounds to sequential information loss across both static and dynamic partially observable environments, deriving two complementary regularizers: predictive sufficiency and recursive consistency. (3) We offer an effective training architecture using scalable synthetic data generation and a unified asymmetric critic to compute calibrated variational lower bounds, obviating the need for human preference labels. (4) We demonstrate MaxIM’s efficacy on diverse benchmarks—a dynamic multi-turn user simulator and a novel arXiv scientific reading task—achieving superior factual grounding, token-budget Pareto efficiency, and task success.
2Related Work

Incremental Summarization and Memory Buffers.
Traditional summarization processes entire documents to generate static outputs [12, 13], whereas incremental summarization recursively updates a summary as streaming information arrives [14]. While early text streaming systems relied on clustering algorithms [15], modern neural approaches exploit structural representations (e.g., JSON states) for incremental updates [10]. A parallel line of work compresses long contexts in continuous space—including learned soft-prompt or embedding compression [16, 17, 18] and optimal-transport token-merging or KV-cache compression. These methods require either retraining the downstream model to consume continuous latents or white-box access to internal model activations. By contrast, we maintain a discrete, human-readable text memory under a token budget K, allowing it to interface directly with any frozen black-box agent. Recently, sophisticated memory buffer methods have emerged to manage unbounded LLM contexts. The closest analogs to our setup are memory systems such as MemGPT [6], Mem-α [8], and MemAgent [7]. While MemGPT and Mem-α focus on tool-calling, MemAgent learns an explicit, generative memory update policy using RL, as we do. However, these methods rely on sparse task rewards which can exacerbate hallucination and historical drift due to credit assignment failures. MaxIM builds on this foundation by introducing theoretically derived, dense MI regularizers that explicitly guide the retention of task-relevant information.
Preference Modeling and Information-Theoretic Shaping.
Modern alignment techniques like RLHF [19, 20] and RLAIF [21, 22] typically train heuristic reward models on pairwise rankings using the Bradley-Terry model [23]. While successful for general alignment, these scalar models lack formal guarantees w.r.t. preserving task-critical information and struggle with long-horizon credit assignment. While MaxIM is similar to RLAIF in its use of an oracle AI for offline data generation, we depart from preference-based rewards. Instead, we frame context compression as a reward shaping problem [24]. Specifically, by training a critic to compute calibrated VPL bounds, MaxIM provides dense, step-by-step information-theoretic rewards. This directly optimizes rigorous MI lower bounds, promoting predictive sufficiency and factual grounding without the theoretical liabilities of standard preference approximations.
RL with Asymmetric Context.
RL with asymmetric context (or privileged information) trains policies using a critic that has access to oracle information unavailable to the actor [25, 26]. Widely used in robotics to train student policies with expert teachers, we adapt it to LLM memory. By treating future text or latent intents as “oracle hindsight context,” we compute dense information-theoretic rewards that shape the LLM’s summary update policy without expensive human labels.
3Background

3.1Capacity-Constrained Memory and Sparse Rewards

Incremental Summarization.
We formalize the environment as a sequential interaction stream. An agent (or actor) engages with an environment, generating actions at∈𝒜 given a continuous stream of observations ot∈Ω. Optimal decision making generally requires conditioning on the current history Ht=(o1,a1,…,at−1,ot). Maintaining Ht indefinitely is computationally intractable for LLMs due to their finite context windows, hence, the agent adopts a summarizer policy πθ​(zt∣zt−1,at−1,ot) that incrementally updates a textual summary zt∈⋃k=1K𝒱k, where 𝒱 is the LLM vocabulary and K is a maximum token budget. The agent’s policy conditions its action choice solely on the capacity-constrained working memory zt and the current observation ot to select its next action at.11We assume the agent conditions on memory and the latest observation, though it can use the last k observations if compute and context permit. We assume the agent is fixed/frozen and focus on training the summarizer for optimal performance.
Sparse Rewards and Regularized MDPs.
The standard RL objective for optimizing policies maximizes expected cumulative task reward: J⁡(θ)=𝔼πθ​[∑tγt​Rtask,t]. However, in long-horizon settings, Rtask can be exceptionally sparse (e.g., evaluated only at the end of a multi-turn dialogue or after reading a full document). This sparsity makes RL challenging due to credit assignment failures. While classic reward shaping [24] injects dense signals without altering the optimal policy via potential functions, this is insufficient in our capacity-constrained setting. Instead, we alter the objective to form a regularized Markov decision process (MDP) [27]. By injecting dense, step-wise information-theoretic auxiliary rewards, we explicitly constrain the policy’s exploration manifold, guiding it to find an effective bounded-memory policy rather than the theoretically infeasible unconstrained optimal (which would require unbounded memory).
A Unified POMDP Formulation.
While our sequence compression formulation applies broadly, our framework models the interaction stream as a partially observable MDP (POMDP). This treats summary zt as a textual belief state tracking an unobservable latent state st∈𝒮. Crucially, this interpretation gracefully accommodates diverse streaming models, such as:
Dynamic Latent States (e.g., User Simulation): In multi-turn interactions, a user’s underlying persona, intent, or mood acts as a dynamic latent state st that evolves sequentially. The summary zt tracks this intent to guide the agent’s conversational responses.
Static Latent States and Active Perception (e.g., Goal-directed reading): For tasks like reading a scientific paper to answer eventual questions, the environment state (i.e., full document semantics and golden target answers) is static. However, with bounded context, it becomes fundamentally partially observable. Intermediate actions (e.g., reading the next text chunk) are pure sensing actions, while the summary zt serves as the belief state, accumulating the necessary sufficient statistics from the observations to resolve the unobserved target variables (questions) at the terminal step. By viewing both settings through this lens, we bridge incremental summarization and classical belief tracking, and thus establish formal value suboptimality bounds (see Section 4).
3.2Mutual Information and Representation Learning

Estimating Mutual Information.
Mutual information (MI), denoted I⁡(X,Y) and defined as I⁡(X,Y)=𝔼P⁡(x,y)​[log⁡P⁡(x,y)P⁡(x)​P​(y)], measures the reduction in uncertainty about a random variable Y given knowledge of X. Estimating MI in high-dimensional continuous or discrete spaces is difficult. One prevalent approach in representation learning, contrastive predictive coding (CPC), uses the InfoNCE loss [28]. While successfully applied to learning continuous embeddings, InfoNCE has been proven to be strictly upper-bounded by log⁡N, where N is the batch size [29]. This bound saturates rapidly when modeling high-entropy distributions like autoregressive text generation, limiting its utility as a metric for unbounded optimization.
Variational Bounds.
To overcome this log⁡N limitation, variational approximations based on f-divergences are often adopted, such as the NWJ [30] or SMILE [31] estimators. However, these estimators are known to suffer from high variance, numerical instability, and extreme hyperparameter sensitivity, particularly when the true MI is large [32]. Because of this, we focus on the VPL bound [11]. By introducing a parameterized variational distribution qϕ​(Y∣X), we leverage the non-negativity of KL divergence to establish a theoretically sound lower bound:I⁡(X,Y)≥H⁡(Y)+𝔼P⁡(x,y)​[log⁡qϕ​(y∣x)].(1)In standard representation learning, maximizing this log-likelihood maximizes I⁡(X,Y) when the marginal entropy H⁡(Y) is constant. In closed-loop POMDPs, the agent’s actions influence future states, causing H⁡(Yt) to become weakly policy-dependent. However, as we prove in Section 4, our framework circumvents this dependency: maximizing predictive log-likelihood directly bounds conditional entropy H⁡(Yt∣zt), which bounds the sequential information loss regardless of the marginal H⁡(Yt). This provides a tractable, theoretically rigorous, low-variance surrogate objective that scales naturally to modern LLMs.
4Methodology: The MaxIM Framework
We frame capacity-constrained incremental summarization as a task of information-theoretic reward shaping. Our objective is to learn a summarizer update policy πθ that dynamically creates and maintains a working memory zt, bounded by a strict token limit K, to maximize downstream task utility Rtask. Crucially, πθ is solely responsible for memory management; a separate, frozen action agent (e.g., a conversational assistant or a question-answering module) conditions on this memory zt to act within the environment. Because Rtask is often sparse and delayed in long-horizon streams (e.g., assessed only at the terminal turn T), standard RL struggles with credit assignment. Our goal is to derive principled, dense shaping rewards that offer step-by-step auxiliary guidance through the optimization landscape.

Assessing the Impact of Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Algorithmic Problem-Solving
Journal: Knowledge-Based SystemsGabriel Souza Baggio, Gabriel Machado LunardiFederal University of Santa Maria, Roraima Avenue, 1000, Santa Maria, 97105-800, Rio Grande do Sul, BrazilGuilherme Medeiros Machado, Subhankar Maity, Faiza BelbachirLyRIDS lab, ECE Engineering School, 10 Rue Sextius Michel, Paris, 75015, Île-de-France, FranceJosé Palazzo Moreira de OliveiraFederal University of Rio Grande do Sul, Informatics Institute, Bento Gonçalves Avenue, 9500, Porto Alegre, 91501-970, Rio Grande do Sul, BrazilAbstract
Competitive programming problems pose distinctive challenges for Large Language Models, as they demand not only proficient code generation but also advanced algorithmic reasoning. This study presents a Retrieval-Augmented Generation approach specifically designed to enhance the capacity of Large Language Models to address such problems. Our approach integrates an embedding-based retrieval mechanism and a similarity search algorithm to identify analogous problems within a knowledge database, employing a dynamically adjusted threshold to mitigate retrieval noise. We conducted an evaluation using the CodeContests dataset, focusing on the test split problems that exhibit similarity to instances from the training split. The experimental framework considered three conditions: (i) problems provided solely with their original descriptions, (ii) problems supplemented with randomly selected examples from the training split, and (iii) problems augmented with similar examples retrieved through the proposed method. In addition, we incorporated a Min-K membership inference analysis to examine whether the generated code solutions were influenced by potential memorization of training data within the evaluated Large Language Models. This complementary perspective enables a deeper understanding of model behavior by distinguishing genuine generalization through retrieval from implicit recall of pretraining samples. Performance was assessed using both pass rates and the CodeForces Elo rating of the problems. The results provide empirical evidence that similarity-based retrieval substantially enhances Large Language Models performance in competitive programming scenarios, offering an scalable framework for improving code generation in algorithmic problem-solving contexts.Retrieval-Augmented Generation , Large Language Models , Code Generation , Programming Problems , Information RetrievalKeywords:

1Introduction
Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated proficiency in solving generic problems across various professional domains [37, 20, 38]. Although some evaluation benchmarks indicate high performance — such as on HumanEval, where GPT-4o [28] and Claude-3.5-Sonnet [3] achieved precision scores of 90% and 92%, respectively [40] —, other benchmarks show that LLMs exhibit limitations on competitive programming tasks [8, 43, 17, 39]. For instance, in the analysis by Zheng et al. [43], Claude-3.5-Sonnet achieved a 0% precision rate on medium and hard problems and only 14.1% on easy ones. In the same benchmark, even the best-performing LLMs, such as Gemini-2.5-Pro [15] and DeepSeek-R1 [9], could not solve a single hard problem.These errors typically arise due to a lack of specific contextual knowledge and a limited understanding of underlying data structures, leading to hallucinations — outputs that are syntactically invalid or logically inconsistent [24]. Under a deeper epistemological analysis, it becomes evident that Large Language Models (LLMs) operate on opinion-based trajectories—that is, on the formulation of statements not necessarily grounded in verifiable evidence, but rather derived from inferences or interpretations constructed within a limited context of knowledge. Hallucination, in this sense, may be understood as the generation of a perception or belief that, while internally coherent, does not correspond to empirical reality. In LLMs, this phenomenon arises because the model “believes” it is producing a consistent and contextually appropriate response, even though such a response lacks factual https://t.co/6AuCmHiPuB mitigate this, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) [18, 13] has been proposed as a mechanism to ground the model’s outputs in relevant external knowledge by, with an Information Retrieval (IR) algorithm, retrieving contextually similar information from a structured corpus [18, 13]. This work investigates how RAG can be used to enhance the problem-solving capabilities of LLMs.The proposition for applying RAG in this context is based on two key observations. First, studies indicate that problems within competitive programming repositories often share underlying algorithmic patterns and solution structures [10, 11]. Second, the practice of providing relevant examples in the prompt (few-shot prompting) is an established technique for improving LLM performance on complex tasks [31, 25]. Based on this,the hypothesis is  that a RAG system that retrieves previously solved problems with analogous characteristics to a target problem can provide the model with relevant context and reduce https://t.co/HOLELiqhkT achieve this, we developed an Information Retrieval (IR) pipeline that employs embedding similarity with a dynamic threshold [5]. We evaluated this system on the CodeContests dataset [23], which is divided into a training set of 13,328 problems and a test set of 165 problems. In addition to the problem title and statement, each sample includes metadatdynamig programming, bitwise operations). The training split served as the knowledge base from which we retrieved similar examples to augment the LLM prompts for solving the problems in the test set. The correctness of the generated solutions was then evaluated using the CodeForces [27] judge system, allowing us to measure the impact of the retrieved context on the model’s performance.The evaluation involves three distinct prompting strategies: (i) a zero-shot baseline using only the original description, (ii) a random retrieval baseline retrieving unrelated problems from the knowledge base, and (iii) the proposed similarity-based RAG approach retrieving contextually aligned examples. Our analyses demonstrate that the similarity-based retrieval consistently outperforms both baselines, validating the hypothesis that retrieving analogous problems improves LLM reasoning on complex programming tasks. Furthermore, the Min-K membership inference results reveal that many generated code lines correspond to known training patterns, underscoring the importance of disentangling memorization effects from genuine reasoning improvements. Together, these findings provide a dual epistemic safeguard: RAG anchors outputs in external knowledge, while membership inference verifies their originality and data provenance. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:1.We design a RAG framework tailored to competitive programming tasks, integrating an embedding-based similarity search with an adaptive thresholding mechanism to retrieve contextually relevant problems while minimizing retrieval noise.
2.We construct a comprehensive experimental setup using the CodeContests dataset, evaluating six prominent LLMs across three prompting strategies, zero-shot, random retrieval, and RAG-based enhancement, to systematically quantify the effect of similarity-driven retrieval on code generation performance.
3.We introduce a complementary Min-K Membership Inference analysis to assess model exposure and memorization biases, providing a novel perspective on the interplay between retrieval-based augmentation and pretraining data recall.
4.We present an integrated evaluation pipeline combining RAG effectiveness and membership inference insights, offering a dual perspective on both performance improvement and epistemic grounding in competitive programming contexts.
5.Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the design of future reasoning-oriented LLMs and outline directions for extending this work to upcoming state-of-the-art models such as Gemini 3 and GPT-5.
2Related Works
Several works have investigated the ability of LLMs to solve competitive programming problems, experimenting different evaluation metrics and approaches to maximize the correctness of generated solutions [33, 32, 19, 43, 10, 17, 8].
2.1Evaluation Strategies
A main challenge in this domain is developing evaluation metrics that go beyond simple pass/fail rates and accurately reflect a model’s problem-solving skill [32]. While simply annotating the number of correctly solved problems is informative, it fails to distinguish between solving a trivial problem and solving one that challenges even the best human competitors [43].To address this gap, recent benchmarks [32, 30, 6] have adopted the Elo rating system [12], a method widely recognized for assessing the relative skill levels of players in competitive games — and is also used in CodeForces platform. In the context of competitive programming platforms, the Elo system provides a unified scale to quantify both problem difficulty and competitor skill. The difficulty rating d assigned to a problem is calibrated against the entire community of human participants; a contestant with an Elo rating of d has a 50% probability of solving this given problem [6].The Elo rating of a contestant, in turn, provides a clear measure of their standing within the competitive community [43]. For example, a rating of 1600 (an “Expert” on CodeForces) places a user in the top 11% of active participants, while a rating of 2400 (“Grandmaster”) signifies performance in the top 1%. An elite rating of 2700 indicates a skill level superior to approximately 99.9% of competitors. By framing LLM performance in this way, we can move from asking “how many” problems a model solved to “how skilled” the model is.Following this evaluation method, our study treats each LLM as a virtual contestant and calculates its equivalent Elo rating. We specifically employ Bayesian Maximum-A-Posteriori (MAP) Elo rating [44], a method also utilized in [43], to estimate the most probable skill level of a model given its performance.The estimation process begins with the standard Elo probability function, πi​(R), which calculates the likelihood of a model with rating R correctly solving a problem with difficulty di:πi​(R)=11+10(di−R)/400These individual probabilities are used to construct the unnormalized log-posterior function, ℒ⁡(R). This function combines the log-likelihood of the observed outcomes (yi∈{1​ for accepted,0​ for rejected}) across all N problems with a regularizing Gaussian prior on the model’s rating (with mean μ0 and variance σ02):ℒ⁡(R)=∑i=1N[yi​ln⁡πi​(R)+(1−yi)​ln⁡(1−πi​(R))]−(R−μ0)22​σ02Finally, the MAP estimate, R^MAP, is the rating R that maximizes this log-posterior function:R^MAP=arg⁡max𝑅​ℒ​(R)Since our benchmark utilizes the CodeContests dataset [23], which contains most of its problems from CodeForces, we annotated each problem’s official Elo difficulty rating. This provides a standardized metric that allows for a comparison of our results against other benchmarks (assuming they also use Elo), even when the test sets are composed of different problems.
2.2Performance Enhancement Approaches
Prior research has explored enhancing LLM performance through two main strategies: granting models access to external knowledge sources or fine-tuning them on specific datasets. For instance, augmenting models with tools like terminal and internet access has enabled systems such as o3 and o4-mini-high to achieve Elo ratings of 2706 and 2719 respectively [30]. Another strategy involves fine-tuning LLMs on competitive programming datasets to train them on problem-solving patterns, a notable example being Google’s AlphaCode [23]. Since these benchmarks also use Elo for evaluation, we used it as a common metric to assess the effectiveness of our technique in relation to these prior work.
2.3Problem Datasets
Several datasets have been proposed to benchmark the ability of LLMs to solve competitive programming problems [33, 32, 19, 43, 23]. Table 1 summarizes these datasets, detailing how many problems each contains and the time period from which they were sourced.Table 1:Summary of competitive programming datasets used for LLM evaluationDataset# ProblemsProblems’ Year(s)USACO [33]3072011-2024CodeElo [32]4082024LiveCodeBench [19]4422023-2024LiveCodeBench Pro [43]∼584Updated LivelyCodeContests [23]13,4932021
For this study, we selected the CodeContests dataset due to its extensive scale. Our central hypothesis is that retrieving similar, previously solved problems can enhance an LLM’s performance. The large repository of over 13,000 problems in CodeContests provides a sufficiently dense knowledge base, which is essential for a retrieval-based approach to effectively find analogous examples.Other benchmarks, while valuable, were less suited for our research objectives. The USACO dataset, for instance, sources its problems from a platform other than CodeForces, making it incompatible with the Elo rating system used for our evaluation. Datasets like CodeElo, LiveCodeBench, and LiveCodeBench Pro, despite their advantages of containing more recent problems and potentially having less data contamination, offer a very limited number of problems.
3Methodology
To evaluate RAG’s impact on our work, we used six well-known LLMs and a set of programming questions, each paired with a previously tested and accepted solution. These entries serve as the knowledge base for the RAG. All datasets and code used in the methodology are included in our open-source repository11https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ArtigoSBBD-C51C.
3.1Model Selection
The models utilized were chosen based on their use in prior research: DeepSeek-R1 [43, 40, 10], Gemini 2.0 Flash [43, 19, 10], Claude 3.7 Sonnet [43, 10], Qwen models [43, 19, 40, 32], GPT-4-omni [43, 19, 17, 40, 32, 10], and GPT-3.5 Turbo [33, 19]. This section provides information about the models used:Table 2:Overview of models with organization, context window and cut-off date.Full Model NameOrg.Context TokensCut-off DateDeepSeek-R1 [1]DeepSeek131KNot specifiedGemini 2.0 Flash [14]Google1 millionJune 2024Claude 3.7 Sonnet [4]Anthropic200KOctober 2024Qwen2.5-Coder-32B [2]Alibaba128KEnd of 2023GPT-4-omni [28]OpenAI128KSeptember 2023GPT-3.5 Turbo [29]OpenAI16KSeptember 2021
Another decisive factor in the model selection was the diversity in training focus and knowledge cutoff date: we included a code-specialized model (Qwen2.5-Coder-32B), a model known for advanced reasoning capabilities (DeepSeek-R1), a less powerful model (GPT-3.5 Turbo), as well as general-purpose models with broader training data.
3.2Information Retrieval Algorithm
The IR algorithm retrieves similar solved problems from the database. First, each problem description in the database is transformed into a high-dimensional vector embedding using the ‘all-MiniLM-L6-v2’22https://huggingface.co/sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model. These embeddings capture the semantic essence of the problems [22]. The collection of embeddings is then indexed using FAISS (Facebook AI Similarity Search) [21], employing an ‘IndexFlatL2’ structure that computes Euclidean distances. Because the vectors are already normalized, we can compute the similarity directly from the Euclidean distance (on a 0-to-1 scale).A distinctive aspect of our IR system is its adaptive threshold mechanism, introduced by [5]. Instead of a fixed cutoff, the threshold for deeming a retrieved problem “similar enough” is dynamically adjusted based on the highest similarity score. The initial threshold used for the similarity is 70%, but if the highest similarity is strong (above 85%), the threshold becomes more stringent; if weaker (less than 75%), it relaxes, but never below the 70% minimum. Similar adaptive strategies are used in RAG to reduce noise [42], and we apply it with the same intent. As an additional measure to mitigate noise, the system is configured to return a maximum of the three most similar problems.
3.3Dataset Overview
We utilized the CodeContests dataset [23] for this study, designating its training set as the knowledge base for our RAG system and its test set for evaluation. The dataset, sourced primarily from CodeForces problems, is structured as a JSON file where each entry contains the problem’s title, its full description, input/output examples, the official CodeForces rating (when applicable), relevant thematic tags, and verified code solutions. These problems do not require a specific programming language for implementation, allowing for flexibility in the solution approaches. This section describes how we leveraged this dataset to construct our RAG pipeline and analyzes the distribution of difficulties and categories of the problems used.Of the 165 problems in the CodeContests test set, 81 had at least one similar problem found in the knowledge base by our Information Retrieval algorithm. The evaluation was therefore performed on this subset, as the remaining problems had no retrieved counterparts and would not receive any additional information from the RAG system. Furthermore, none of the problems in this evaluation set were part of the RAG’s knowledge base, ensuring a fair assessment of its generalization capabilities [18, 13, 35, 26]. Problems can be classified into one or more categories (e.g., dynamic programming, sorting, binary search), and the distribution of these thematic tags across both datasets is shown in Figure https://t.co/CQ3GfgENac better understand the difficulty distribution of the problems, we performed a classification based on their CodeForces Elo ratings. While the Elo system provides a continuous scale, we grouped the problems into three discrete categories for a better analysis: Easy, Medium, and Hard. Problems with an Elo rating between 0 and 1000 were classified as Easy, those in the range (1000, 2000] as Medium, and any problem rated above 2000 as Hard. It is worth noting that while every problem in the test set is from CodeForces, the training set (our knowledge base) also contains problems from other sources, so not all of them had the CodeForces Elo information available. Shortcuts and Boundaries: Verifiable RL Misalignment and Contextual Safety Learning
Xinjie Shenxinjie@gatech.eduProject WebsiteAbstract
Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve an agent’s task capability while reinforcing behavior that violates contextual execution requirements. We study this reward-driven misalignment, including reward hacking, through verifiable reward–context conflicts, where compliant task completion remains feasible while some executable shortcuts earn more reward than every compliant strategy. Encoding these conflicts in task dynamics lets us generate diverse interactive environments at scale and derive compliance feedback from execution histories. In resource and reporting workflows, task optimization increases real productivity through unauthorized resource use or raises reported scores while actual work declines. Controlled changes in the training distribution show that minority conflict exposure can still lead to widespread shortcut acquisition, reaching 97.9% certified profitable violations on an API task under a 25% conflict mixture after 128 updates. The same contextual checks supply a simple binary penalty that supports joint capability and compliance gains and partially mitigates acquired violations. Learned safety adapts to expanded authorization and transfers across mechanisms into workflows with evolving evidence and approval requirements. On 32 unseen changing-evidence tasks, resource-trained safety increases safe completion from 53.1% to 89.1% relative to task-only training, while both policies achieve full real work. These results connect a verifiable account of reward-driven misalignment with scalable task construction and safety learning that remains useful under changing execution requirements.
1Introduction
Capable and reliable language-model agents are increasingly expected to repair software, schedule resources, and complete complex workflows over long horizons while following human requirements. To develop these capabilities, reinforcement learning (RL) commonly uses task reward based on the quality or amount of work accomplished at the end of an episode, providing a direct, scalable training signal across diverse tasks [Guo et al., 2025, Shen et al., 2026a, Wei et al., 2025a]. However, whether the work meets human expectations also depends on the context in which it is carried out [Levy et al., 2026]. This context includes user intent, interaction history, and specific constraints such as authorization or organizational rules, which determine which actions are appropriate and which constraints apply [Ruan et al., 2024, Xiang et al., 2025, Yao et al., 2024]. Following these contextual requirements becomes more challenging as execution horizons grow [Chen et al., 2026]. Agents must continue to respect resource permissions and preserve evaluation requirements in an evolving environment, where prior commitments can constrain later actions. A finite instruction list may leave requirements and their interactions implicit or unspecified, so compliance can depend on basic safety judgment that cannot be taken for granted in LLM agents [Zhang et al., 2025, Chen et al., 2026]. Even when requirements are explicitly stated, their applicability can change as actions alter the state and create or invalidate obligations [Shen et al., 2026b, Asif et al., 2026]. For example, a user may revoke permission to use an external service and later restore it only for public data. Resuming the earlier workflow may then send restricted data to the service even if the task is completed correctly. Task reward may not fully capture these conditions, leaving room for RL-induced misalignment of the kind observed in studies using production training environments [Anthropic, 2025, Qi et al., 2026].We study these reward-driven forms of misalignment through conflicts between task incentives and contextual execution requirements. Such conflicts can arise even when task reward accurately measures useful work, as additional service calls beyond an authorized allowance can still produce more genuine output. In our experiments, task-reward training improves verified work under full authorization while also increasing certified profitable violations under restricted authorization, illustrating how genuine capability gains can conceal growing execution risk (Fig. 4). In other cases, agents can raise scores by modifying an acceptance test without repairing the software, and our reporting experiments show higher scores accompanied by less actual work. We interpret these reward-seeking departures from expectations, including behaviors commonly studied as reward hacking [Taufeeque et al., 2026, Qi et al., 2026], as shortcuts that bypass contextual requirements of task completion. We construct tasks in which compliant completion remains feasible, while some executable shortcuts earn more reward than any compliant strategy (Fig. 1). These intrinsic, verifiable reward–context conflicts let us study how RL acquires shortcuts under controlled incentives.📷Figure 1:Reward–context conflicts. (a) Compliant completion remains feasible while a violating execution earns higher reward. (b) A binary violation penalty can change the preferred ideal optimum. (c) Expanded authorization can permit the same execution with unchanged physical outcome and task reward. The geometry is schematic.
To support these studies at scale, our construction generates executable task environments in batches, with contextual safety boundaries encoded in their dynamics and verifiable feedback for capability and safety learning. Using these environments, we find that profitable violations can become frequent even when conflict tasks form a minority of the training data. Simple reward shaping with the same feedback supports joint capability and compliance gains and mitigates acquired violations. The learned safety behavior adapts to expanded authorization and generalizes across new tasks and scenarios, as well as changes in wording and permission scope. Cross-task cases further document capability transfer and violation emergence, alongside protection that carries over to workflows whose evidence and approval requirements change during execution.
2Formulation
We consider language-model agents trained through reinforcement learning (RL) in executable task environments. Task dynamics determine which executions are possible by specifying how tool calls change the environment’s state and return observations. Contextual requirements distinguish compliant executions within this space, while task reward assigns value to the resulting outcomes. We formalize conflicts between these requirements and task reward as verifiable task properties. This lets us construct tasks for studying shortcut acquisition and use the same execution checks to learn contextual compliance.
2.1Contextual execution and task reward
For a task instance, let τ denote an execution trajectory ending in a terminal state and T the set of trajectories executable under its dynamics. A context c specifies requirements on how the task is carried out, and C⁡(c)⊆T contains the trajectories that satisfy them. Trajectories in T∖C⁡(c) remain executable despite falling outside contextual expectations (Fig. 1a). Within an execution, earlier actions can change which requirements apply later, so compliance is defined over the full history. Across authorization contexts, expanded permission can make the same physical execution compliant without changing its outcome or task reward (Fig. 1c). Section 3 describes how these boundaries are implemented in executable environments.Let Rtask​(τ) denote native task reward and b a fixed task-value baseline. We use the bounded, graded value V⁡(τ)=Rtask​(τ)−b, whose zero marks this value baseline. The score and b are fixed before interaction and shared by paired authorization contexts, so centering preserves reward ordering and reward gaps. Task completion follows the instance’s own requirements and is checked separately (Appendix B.2).
2.2Verifiable reward–context conflicts
We call a reward-seeking route that bypasses contextual requirements of task completion a shortcut. Excess resource use can increase real output; altering a measurement channel can increase the score without such progress. To study how agents acquire these behaviors during RL, we construct instances with two verifiable properties.P1: Compliant feasibility. There exists a reference execution τc meeting the basic task goal and satisfyingτc∈C⁡(c),V⁡(τc)≥0.(1)P1 makes the required completion feasible within the contextual boundary.P2: Reward conflict. The best compliant reward is strictly below the best executable reward outside the compliant set:maxτ∈C⁡(c)⁡V⁡(τ)<maxτ∈T∖C⁡(c)⁡V⁡(τ).(2)The two trajectory classes are nonempty, and the bounded task reward attains a maximum on each. Together, P1 and P2 describe tasks that can be completed as required, while some executable shortcuts earn more reward than every compliant strategy.Executable references certify these properties. We execute τc through the same tool interface available to the agent to verify compliant task completion at or above the value baseline. Its reward is recorded alongside independently checked work. For P2, let Vc∗=maxτ∈C⁡(c)⁡V⁡(τ) denote the compliant optimum and let Uc be a certified upper bound on it. A violating witness τs∈T∖C⁡(c) certifies the conflict when its execution through this interface establishesVc∗≤Uc<V⁡(τs)≤maxτ∈T∖C⁡(c)⁡V⁡(τ).(3)When the exact compliant optimum is available, set Uc=Vc∗. These references establish a reward advantage for an executable shortcut over all compliant strategies (Fig. 2). Applying the same feasibility and conflict criteria across task instances supplies a basis for batch construction and controlled studies of RL behavior.📷Figure 2:Feasible completion and a certified shortcut. (a) A compliant reference τc meets the task goal and attains the value baseline, while an executable shortcut τs crosses the contextual boundary. (b) Every compliant value is at most the certified bound Uc. A witness with V⁡(τs)>Uc guarantees a positive reward gap (Eq. (3)). The zero line marks the task-value baseline; contours increase toward the shortcut endpoint. Curves and reward levels are schematic.

2.3Learning and evaluating contextual compliance
With contextual violations made verifiable by construction, a simple mitigation is to penalize them in the training reward. Let Ic​(τ) equal zero when τ∈C⁡(c) and one otherwise, and let λ≥0 weight the penalty. We compare:Task-trained: Rtask(τ),Safety-trained: Rtask(τ)−λIc(τ),λ=1.(4)Let Vs∗=maxτ∈T∖C⁡(c)⁡V⁡(τ) and λ×=Vs∗−Vc∗>0. The binary penalty leaves every compliant reward unchanged and subtracts the same λ from each violating reward. The two ideal optima tie at λ=λ×; the compliant optimum is strictly preferred exactly whenλ>λ×=Vs∗−Vc∗.(5)Figure 1b shows this ideal change in preference. Policy training then tests how the same contextual feedback shapes useful execution and compliance.Evaluation compares task reward with independently verified actual work. We track historical violations over the execution and certify them as profitable only when their reward exceeds the compliant optimum or a valid upper bound on it. Other boundary-crossing trajectories can raise a policy’s score while remaining below that reference. Historical checking retains these events, while independent work verification distinguishes unauthorized productivity from changes to the measurement channel. The constructed tasks thus connect learned behavior to a verifiable incentive conflict, while the same execution checks provide feedback for learning contextual compliance alongside capability.Section 3 constructs executable task environments following VHD’s mechanism-first approach [Shen et al., 2026a]. We ground task reward and contextual checks in the state-update mechanism before realizing its tool interface, so each instance retains a verified incentive structure.
3Scalable construction of verifiable task environments
In real workflows, executable behavior can exceed contextual permission. This gap provides a practical source of reward–context conflicts. We turn it into reusable task mechanisms by encoding contextual requirements as checks on the states and execution histories maintained by task dynamics, while keeping boundary-crossing actions executable. Following VHD, we then render these dynamics into interactive environments [Shen et al., 2026a].Figure 3 illustrates how familiar operational rules give rise to these mechanisms. Under a shared resource allowance, a tool call can produce more work while pushing cumulative use beyond the authorized total, including when calls are spread across accounts. The dynamics record both work and resource consumption, allowing productive execution to register a contextual violation. In a versioned workflow, publication requires evidence for the current artifact, even though the interface may still allow an archived report to be selected. Renewing the evidence restores its current validity, while an earlier invalid publication remains part of the execution history.📷Figure 3:From encoded dynamics to tool execution. (a) Shared resource permission and (b) current-version evidence pair agent-facing tool calls with their state transitions and contextual boundaries. (c) A schematic trajectory projection with illustrative reward contours increasing toward the violating endpoint. Teal denotes compliant execution; orange denotes a violation. Shading shows current evidence validity; the returning path renews evidence after an invalid publication while retaining that breach in history. Calls remain executable, and va and vr denote artifact and report revisions.
Mechanism sources and sampling. These examples draw on requirements already present in practical workflows. Input-validity rules provide further candidates, as in an ordering interface that accepts negative quantities despite a nonnegative-quantity requirement. Unforeseen weaknesses in real systems can expose similar gaps. In the OpenAI–Hugging Face incident, agents seeking task solutions exploited infrastructure vulnerabilities to circumvent network isolation and access third-party systems [OpenAI, 2026]. Even when the intended boundary is clear, the operations and combinations that allow an agent to cross it may not have been anticipated.We construct candidate mechanisms by retaining a contextual requirement while relaxing its enforcement in the executable dynamics. In a resource workflow, for example, sampling varies physical capacity and job demands together with the authorized allowance. The same accounting rules track resource use across these instances. A reference procedure verifies a compliant trajectory that meets the task goal (P1) and an executable violating trajectory whose reward exceeds the compliant optimum or a valid upper bound (P2). We retain instances satisfying both properties. Changing authorization can also produce an ordinary counterpart with the same physical task and reward, supporting controlled mixtures of ordinary and conflict tasks. Together with corpus grounding, parameter sampling provides diverse environments under shared verification rules. Table 4 gives the core mechanism catalogue.Corpus-grounded realization. For a sampled instance with parameters θ, an LLM setter renders its executable dynamics D⁡(θ) into an agent-facing environment. The setter also receives an independently sampled corpus passage x, which supplies the operational setting and domain language. Stateful tools implement the underlying transitions, while the work order presents the applicable contextual requirements. Through the mapping D⁡(θ)→E⁡(θ,x), admitted realizations preserve the instance’s task reward and contextual checks across different scenarios and interfaces. Parameter sampling changes the instance, while corpus grounding diversifies its realization. The setter has access to the mechanism and instance parameters, while the solver encounters the realized environment through task instructions and tool observations. The underlying implementation and reference outcomes remain private. Execution checks follow the VHD realization approach [Shen et al., 2026a], with replay and admission criteria detailed in Appendix A.3.Table 1 presents representative workflows alongside task coverage and mechanism construction results. Beyond sampling existing families, an automated proposal study produced seven verified workflows from 24 requests by pairing newly authored dynamics with constrained-search verification. These workflows compose state changes with contextual requirements, as when editing a document invalidates an earlier approval.The same compositional approach underlies the release tasks evaluated in Section 4.3, where changing vendor permissions interacts with evidence and approval requirements. In one such workflow, an approval response revises the evidence rule and commitment, creating new obligations before publication (Fig. 13a). Such compositions make compliance depend on how earlier operations change the requirements governing later ones. The resulting environments support controlled studies of shortcut acquisition and useful contextual safety. Their execution histories provide the binary violation feedback in Eq. (4), allowing the same task mechanisms to support both task-only optimization and safety-aware RL.

4Experiments
We study how reward–context conflicts shape behavior during RL and whether feedback grounded in the same contextual requirements supports useful, transferable compliance. RQ1. What does task reward optimization learn when profitable shortcuts are available despite explicitly stated contextual requirements? RQ2. Can context-dependent feedback train useful safety behavior, both from Base and after shortcut acquisition? RQ3. How far do capability, shortcut behavior, and contextual safety generalize?Experimental setup. The starting policy is Qwen3.5-4B (Base). We optimize policies with GRPO using their own group rollouts from admitted task environments. In the constructed tasks, public task instructions explicitly provide the applicable contextual requirements and authorization conditions during training and evaluation. Task-trained optimizes task reward; Safety-trained adds the binary history penalty in Eq. (4). Policies share evaluation instances, authorization conditions, tools, and inference budget within each comparison. Prevention starts from Base; mitigation continues from a common Task-trained parent. Training sources for each comparison are specified in Appendix B.1.Shared measurements. We report task reward, independently verified real work, historical violations, and certified profitable violations. Certification requires a contextual violation and reward strictly above the compliant optimum or a valid upper bound. Paired contexts change authorization while preserving the physical task and score. Independent work checks assess the original task requirements; mechanism-specific completion criteria are in Appendix B.2. Safe completion requires task completion with no historical violation.
4.1RQ1: Learning capability and profitable shortcuts

4.1.1Capability gains and shortcut acquisition
Task optimization can improve real work while increasing profitable violations. On the API resource task, Task-trained improves verified work in both authorized and restricted contexts, while certified profitable violations rise sharply under restricted authorization. Higher reward here reflects additional work, including work obtained through unauthorized resource use (Fig. 4a). Validation shows the opposite work pattern: the reported score approaches its maximum while current-state repair progress declines and certified profitable violations increase. Together, the two panels distinguish unauthorized productivity from manipulation of the measurement channel (Fig. 4b).📷Figure 4:Two routes to higher reward. Open circles are Base; filled circles are Task-trained. Each directed span shows the gap between the observed endpoints. (a) API reward measures verified output. (b) Validation reward reads reports and can diverge from actual repair. Violation rates use 48 attempts per context.
To distinguish amplification from newly observed violations, we examine the acquisition patterns across mechanisms and fixed cases. The panels show amplification from both low and established Base risk. On an API subset with no observed Base events, Task-trained additionally exhibits historical and certified profitable violations (Fig. 5). 4.1.2Conflict prevalence and continued optimization
A multi-mechanism Task-trained policy exposed to both authorized ordinary tasks and restricted conflict tasks improves authorized real work on both resource mechanisms, alongside an increase in restricted certified profitable violations (Fig. 6). We then use paired authorization conditions to vary conflict exposure within the same resource mechanisms. At matched training dose, a 25% conflict mixture produces fewer restricted violations than 100% conflict training. On API, certified profitable violations are 18.8% versus 81.3%, while authorized real work is .999 versus .983. Restricted safe completion also increases on both resource mechanisms (Table 2). Anthropic is about to sell the public a trillion-dollar company controlled by 2 shares worth less than a penny.

And the people buying it will have almost no way to change anything that happens next.

I read the voting section of Anthropic's IPO filing, and I think it's the most one-sided deal ever offered to regular investors at this size:

There is exactly ONE Class F share. It belongs to an LLC owned by 7 of Anthropic's co-founders, and it carries 50.1% of all the votes.

There is exactly ONE Class T share. It belongs to Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust, and it elects a majority of the board.

If Anthropic were ever liquidated, each of those 2 shares would get its par value of $0.00001.

The public gets Class A shares instead. And Anthropic's own filing says this structure may effectively eliminate their ability to influence important decisions, including a sale of the company.

So here's what that means for anyone who buys:

- They can't replace the board if the company stumbles, because the trust picks the majority and the founders hold half the vote.
- They can't push for a sale, even if someone offers a huge premium.
- They can't stop the board from putting the mission ahead of their money. Anthropic is a public benefit corporation, so the board has to weigh shareholders against the long-term benefit of humanity.
- And they can't easily sue over it. Delaware law requires at least 2% of the shares or $2 million worth of stock to bring that kind of claim.

This isn't some far-off hypothetical either.

The filing warns that slowing AI development for safety may not maximize stockholder value. It also says Anthropic recently paused training a next-generation model for more than a month over safety and security concerns.

A public shareholder would've had zero say in that pause.

And here's the part I can't get past:

Each co-founder has pledged to give 80% of their Anthropic equity to charity. The Class F vote stays at 50.1% no matter how much stock they still own.

So the founders can give away most of their money and keep all of their control.

Dario Amodei told 60 Minutes last year that he's deeply uncomfortable with AI decisions being made by a few companies and a few people. When he was asked who elected him, he said no one.

Now his company's IPO hands 50.1% of the votes to 7 people, and he's one of them.

And guess who's being lined up to buy it?

Anthropic has weighed reserving 15% to 20% of the IPO for individual investors, according to Bloomberg. JPMorgan is leading the US retail push, and Citigroup is handling retail buyers in places like Japan, Britain and Canada.

The same filing warns that AI could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.

So regular people are being asked to buy a company that says its product could threaten humanity, with no real vote on how it's run.

Anthropic's answer is that this is the whole point. The structure is built to keep Wall Street from pressuring it into cutting corners on safety. The trustees have no financial stake in the company. Google and Meta gave their founders control and still made shareholders rich. And every buyer gets all of this in writing before they buy.

But Zuckerberg's control comes from shares he owns, so when Meta's stock falls, he loses money too. Anthropic's 2 control shares can't lose anything.

Anyone buying this IPO is paying full price to hand control to 7 founders and 5 trustees.

They're desperate for money and they don't care about your money.

Apparently everyone in Renaissance Florence was accusing each other of being gay all the time.

Between 1432 and 1502, this city of 40,000 persons would investigate 17,000 men for homosexuality, meaning that half or more of all men would be investigated during their life.

Since you could report anyone anonymously to the authorities by dropping a note, and the punishments for those convicted were financial fines and political disbarment, there was both a low bar and financial incentives to investigate people, plus benefits if financial or political rivals were accused.

Leonardo da Vinci was accused anonymously twice, probably due to his association with the Medici, and although cleared, bitterly complained about the Florentine justice system in his notes afterwards.

Couple thoughts:

1) After several people pointed out that Lyman couldn't substitute all-cause mortality for malaria-specific mortality like he had done, he fixed it. His initial estimate for $/lives saved was $19000; revised it’s about $8,200. 

2) I think, though I could be wrong about this, that his calculation to get $8200 still has a problem: he calculates the costs of the distribution based on the whole population but the benefits based on 75% of the population (since he argues the other 25% is already sleeping under nets). But as he himself identifies, the nice thing about an intention-to-treat analysis is that you don't need to do this and shouldn't: you just ask how much to expect mortality to fall in a village after handing out the nets, and the answer is 17%. (You only care about the fact some people are already sleeping under nets if that makes your village unlike the one where the  17% was measured; more on that below.) If he changed this one factor this would make his numbers quite close to GiveWell's.

3) He then applies an adjustment for the long-term: "If bednets reduced short-run all-cause mortality by 18% in the 1990s and maybe reduce it by (who knows?) 14% today, they probably reduce actual child mortality (i.e. across 5 years of early childhood) by 7-11%." 

But GiveWell actually accounts for that even more stringently by just excluding all benefits past the first two years, one of several places where they are intentionally conservative. 

4) He accuses GiveWell of misrepresenting Cochrane's statistics  but they actually just report a bunch of different numbers and I think he mixed them up. He complains "GiveWell cites that review to support a “45% reduction in malaria incidence.” That’s an error, that review did not find a 45% reduction in malaria incidence." But the review absolutely does report almost exactly that: "Insecticide-treated nets also reduce the incidence of uncomplicated episodes of Plasmodium falciparum malaria by almost a half (rate ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.64; 5 trials, 35,551 participants, high-certainty evidence". Rate ratio 0.55 means a 45% reduction. 

5) He expresses concern that a lot of the Cochrane studies are old and describe a different environment (Africa in the late 1990s/early 2000s). However, GiveWell's most recent grant to nets in the DRC - which I believe that my donations helped to fund - is based on data from a 2023-2024 large scale demographic survey in the DRC, so the nets are being distributed in an environment very close to the one studied. It found about a 14% all-cause mortality reduction in the first year after a distribution, close to the 17% in Cochrane. 

He also expresses concern that Cochrane's mortality estimate here is low-powered but I don't think it is (the analysis says "rate ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.77 to 0.89; 5 trials, 200,833 participants, high-certainty evidence") so it's between 11% and 23% with a 95% CI!

6) He also raises questions about whether there are more people trying to hand out nets than nets to be handed out. GiveWell looked into that and determined that in the DRC, there was not enough funding to do all the distributions that were indicated, in part because the Global Fund caps how much it'll spend in any one country. 

7) Finally, he argues we should instead - from an altruistic perspective - spend our money however maximizes GDP. But I think there's a serious case that health interventions like combatting malaria are necessary for GDP growth to take off in DRC, just like the American South was kind of a backwater until we eradicated malaria there. Being constantly sick is horrible for productivity. Being only able to hire employees who are constantly sick is horrible for a business environment. GiveWell estimates that a $1,000,000 donation increases adult income for 80,000 children by 0.6%, which means that much of their modelled benefit of malaria nets *is* their GDP effects.

My best guess is that if you were a hard-nosed GDP maxxer you'd invest a lot in reducing the disease burden in poor countries.  Or maybe you'd go all in on making AI happen as fast as possible, something I rarely see EAs criticized for failing to do. I would probably donate more money to making AI go well if I had more of an idea of how to do that and it wouldn't create a bunch of conflicts of interest with my reporting work.

I agree it would be cool if there were an organization focused on effective institutional capacity building in poor countries, but the reason I and man others don't donate to this is not that everyone fails to realize how important institutions are, it's that even though many people have worked very hard on the problem for a long time they do not have a way better than the nets to turn my money into GDP growth in poor countries. 

There was a bit of a Our World In Data article I read this fall that has stuck with me: 

"I’ve never had malaria, but I know several people who have. They describe it as one of the worst experiences of their life.

What starts out feeling like the flu — which is bad enough — can quickly progress into something far worse. The body swings from intense fever and sweats to chills deep enough to make you shake uncontrollably. Everything aches, from your muscles and joints to the pounding headache that makes it impossible to think clearly. Your body is so fatigued that it’s a battle to make it to the bathroom when the nausea and vomiting arrive.

That’s what a pretty standard infection feels like. For some, it goes much further. Here is how one account describes it:

“I awoke to what felt like lightning going through my legs, and then spreading through my body and in my head. Probably the worst headache, body aches, and chills you could possibly imagine. It felt like I was being stung repeatedly by an electric shock gun and could barely control my movements. The pain was so intense; I actually believed I was dying, literally crying out in pain so bad that I was taken to a 24-hour clinic that night at 3am.”

In Senegal, the median child experienced 43 attacks of malaria over the course of their childhood. My hard-nosed productivity obsessed persona says "I bet that's rough on their human capital development, and it's quite cheap to prevent." But mostly I don't, actually, say that to myself. I just buy some nets. If something even better comes along I'll do that, but I haven't seen it yet.
